rows.claim: This Lesson distils the Preface and Chapters 1 and 2: zero to one, the contrarian question and the dot-com lessons. It matters because your AI product builds ownership only if it creates something new.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Contents page of the text: "Preface: Zero to One / 1 The Challenge of the Future / 2 Party Like It's 1999". The contrarian question opens Chapter 1; the dot-com lessons are in Chapter 2.

rows.claim: Going from 0 to 1 means doing something new, vertical or intensive progress. Going from 1 to n means copying what works, horizontal or extensive progress.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 1: "Horizontal or extensive progress means copying things that work--going from 1 to n ... Vertical or intensive progress means doing new things--going from 0 to 1."

rows.claim: Chapter 2, Party Like It's 1999: after the dot-com crash, founders took four lessons. Make incremental advances, stay lean and flexible, improve on the competition, and focus on product over sales.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 2 lists four lessons: "1. Make incremental advances 2. Stay lean and flexible 3. Improve on the competition 4. Focus on product, not sales".

rows.claim: Before you pick your AI product, write your answer to Thiel's question: what valuable thing is nobody building? If ten tools already do it, you are going from 1 to n.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 3 gives the business version as "what valuable company is nobody building?". The Card said "valuable thing"; changed to "valuable company" in en and fa. The "ten tools" line is the app's own application, not a book figure.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Chapters 3 to 5: why monopoly beats competition and the traits that make a monopoly last. It matters because a small AI product earns ownership income only if it escapes copycats.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Contents: "3 All Happy Companies Are Different / 4 The Ideology of Competition / 5 Last Mover Advantage". Monopoly traits are in Chapter 5.

rows.claim: Under perfect competition, the economists' ideal, no company makes an economic profit. In 2012 US airlines earned about 37 cents per passenger trip, while Google kept a 21 percent margin.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 3: "in 2012, when the average airfare each way was $178, the airlines made only 37 cents per passenger trip ... Google brought in $50 billion in 2012 ... but it kept 21% of those revenues as profits"; "Under perfect competition, in the long run no company makes an economic profit." Both open audit figures (37 cents, 21 percent) confirmed.

rows.claim: Chapter 5, Last Mover Advantage: a business is worth its future cash flows. For a tech company, most of that value comes at least 10 to 15 years in the future.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 5: "the value of a business today is the sum of all the money it will make in the future"; "Most of a tech company's value will come at least 10 to 15 years in the future."

rows.claim: Trait one, proprietary technology: it should be at least 10x better than its closest substitute. Google search and Amazon offering far more books are his examples.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 5: "proprietary technology must be at least 10 times better than its closest substitute in some important dimension"; "Google's search algorithms, for example, return results better than anyone else's"; Amazon "offered at least 10 times as many books as any other bookstore".

rows.claim: For your AI product, pick one job and one kind of user, and aim to be 10x better than their current workaround. Scale only after you own that niche.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. The 10x figure is the book's (Ch. 5: "at least 10 times better than its closest substitute"; "once you're 10x better, you escape competition"). The rest is the app's own application.

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Chapters 7, 8 and 13: the power law, secrets and the seven questions. It matters because your satellite bets and your startup choice follow the same few-big-wins math.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Contents: "7 Follow the Money / 8 Secrets / 13 Seeing Green". The power law is Chapter 7; the seven questions are in Chapter 13.

rows.claim: Apply the power law to your 20 percent satellite: one or two bets may return more than all the others. Size each bet so losing it does not touch your index core.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 7: venture returns "follow a power law: a small handful of companies radically outperform all others". The 20 percent satellite is the app's own portfolio frame, not a figure from the book, and the Card does not attribute it to Thiel.

rows.claim: Durability: will your market position be defensible 10 and 20 years into the future? The secret: have you found a unique opportunity that others do not see?
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 13: "6. The Durability Question: Will your market position be defensible 10 and 20 years into the future? 7. The Secret Question: Have you identified a unique opportunity that others don't see?"

rows.claim: This Lesson distils Chapters 9 to 11: foundations, the PayPal mafia and distribution. It matters because your AI product fails if early choices on partners or selling go wrong.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Contents: "9 Foundations / 10 The Mechanics of Mafia / 11 If You Build It, Will They Come?". "PayPal Mafia" appears in Chapter 10.

rows.claim: Everyone involved should be fully committed, ideally full time. Thiel says the CEO of an early-stage, venture-backed startup should never get more than 150,000 dollars a year in salary.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 9: "As a general rule, everyone you involve with your company should be involved full-time"; "In no case should a CEO of an early-stage, venture-backed startup receive more than $150,000 per year in salary."

rows.claim: You should be able to explain why your 20th employee would join you instead of a bigger company. Good answers are about your mission and your team, not perks like free laundry pickup.
rows.note: Read in a full-text copy of the book that is not an authorised source, so it is not linked; the link is the catalogue entry for the book. Ch. 10: "Why should the 20th employee join your company?"; good answers are "answers about your mission and answers about your team"; "Anybody who would be more powerfully swayed by free laundry pickup or pet day care would be a bad addition to your team."
